title: Code from Bed
outcome: Go from never having written code to shipping and maintaining a real web application you built, understand and can change.

phases.name: Starting From Nothing
phases.outcome: Get a working setup, write and run your first real code, and read an error message without panic.

modules.name: What Code Actually Is
modules.objective: Explain what code is, who it's written for, and what a computer does with it.
lessons: Instructions, written by humans, for humans
What actually happens when you run a program
Languages: why there are so many and why it barely matters yet
The gap between knowing and doing, and how to close it
Learning to code with a body that has opinions
practice: Predict what eight tiny programs will print
lab: Write down what you want to build by the end
A written goal with three things you'd like to make, and why each one

modules.name: A Setup That Works From Bed
modules.objective: Get a working coding environment you can use lying down, on a phone if needed.
lessons: Browser-based editors: coding with nothing installed
Installing an editor properly, when you're ready
The terminal: five commands and no more for now
Files, folders and where your code actually lives
Setting up for low light, low energy and one hand
practice: Complete seven setup tasks in a browser editor
lab: Build the setup you'll use for the rest of the track
A working environment, documented, that you can start in under a minute

modules.name: Your First Programs
modules.objective: Write, run and change small programs that produce visible output.
lessons: Output: making the computer say something
Changing a program and predicting the change first
Comments, and writing them for the you of next week
Breaking a program on purpose to see what happens
Typing less: snippets, autocomplete and copy-paste discipline
practice: Modify eight programs to produce a stated output
lab: Write a program that introduces you
A running program that prints a formatted introduction you wrote yourself

modules.name: Errors Are Information
modules.objective: Read an error message, find the line it means, and fix it without guessing.
lessons: The error message is talking to you, in order
Syntax errors: the computer literally can't read it
Runtime errors: it read it and then it went wrong
The stack trace, from the bottom up
practice: Fix eight broken programs from the error alone
lab: Debug a program with five deliberate faults
A working program plus a note on what each error message told you

modules.name: Asking an AI for Help, Well
modules.objective: Get useful coding help from an AI tool and check the answer before trusting it.
lessons: What to include so the answer is about your problem
Asking for an explanation, not just a fix
Checking an answer you don't fully understand yet
When the AI is confidently wrong, and how you'd know
Learning from the answer instead of pasting it
practice: Improve seven weak help requests
lab: Solve a problem with AI help and explain the solution
A working solution plus your own explanation of how it works, in your words

phases.name: The Building Blocks
phases.outcome: Use variables, types, conditions, loops, functions and data structures to solve real small problems.

modules.name: Variables and Types
modules.objective: Store, name and change values, and know what kind of value you're holding.
lessons: A variable is a name for a value
Numbers, text and true/false: the three you need first
Names that tell the next reader what this is
practice: Fix the type bug in eight snippets
lab: Model something real as a set of variables
A program describing a real object with well-named, correctly-typed variables

modules.name: Making Decisions
modules.objective: Write code that behaves differently depending on the situation.
lessons: If, else, and the question in between
Comparison, equality and the one that catches everyone
Nested conditions and when to stop nesting
The case you forgot: thinking about all the branches
practice: Complete eight decision problems
lab: Build a decision tool for a real question you have
A working tool that takes inputs and gives a reasoned answer

modules.name: Doing Things Repeatedly
modules.objective: Repeat work without repeating yourself, and stop when you should.
lessons: Loops: the same work over many items
Looping a known number of times
Looping until something is true, and the one that never ends
Breaking out early and skipping an item
Building something up as you loop
practice: Write eight loops from a stated result
lab: Process a real list of your own data
A program that reads a list you supply and produces a useful summary

modules.name: Functions
modules.objective: Package work into named, reusable pieces with clear inputs and outputs.
lessons: A function is a named piece of work
Arguments: what it needs to do its job
Return values, and the function that returns nothing
Turning repeated code into a function
practice: Extract functions from eight repetitive programs
lab: Refactor your loop project into functions
The same program, rewritten as named functions, still working

modules.name: Lists and Records
modules.objective: Hold collections of things and structured records, and get data back out of them.
lessons: Lists: many values under one name
Getting items out, and the index that's off by one
Records: describing one thing with named fields
Lists of records, which is most real data
Choosing the right shape for your data
practice: Restructure eight badly-shaped datasets
lab: Build a small searchable collection
A program holding a list of records that can filter and sort them

phases.name: Making Things People Can See
phases.outcome: Build web pages that look right, respond to input, and work for everyone.

modules.name: HTML: Structure and Meaning
modules.objective: Build a page whose structure describes what the content actually is.
lessons: A page is a document with structure
Semantic elements, and why div isn't the answer
Images, alt text and the description that carries meaning
Forms: asking the user for something
practice: Fix the semantics of eight markup snippets
lab: Build a semantic page about something you care about
A page that reads correctly with a screen reader and headings turned into an outline

modules.name: CSS: Making It Look Right
modules.objective: Style a page deliberately instead of by trial and error.
lessons: The box model, which explains most confusion
Layout with flexbox, without memorising everything
Colour, contrast and text that people can actually read
Responsive: the same page on a phone in bed
practice: Achieve eight stated layouts
lab: Style your page to a stated design
A styled page meeting contrast requirements and working at 400% zoom

modules.name: JavaScript in the Page
modules.objective: Make a page respond to what the user does.
lessons: Finding an element and changing it
Events: responding to a click or a keypress
Reading what someone typed into a form
Showing and hiding without breaking screen readers
Keeping the page usable by keyboard
practice: Wire up eight interactions
lab: Make your page interactive
An interactive page that works fully by keyboard alone

modules.name: Remembering Things
modules.objective: Save and reload data so a page remembers between visits.
lessons: JSON: the shape data travels in
Loading saved data and handling none being there
What should never go in browser storage
Data that survives a corrupted save
practice: Add persistence to seven small apps
lab: Add saving to your interactive page
A page that remembers state across reloads and survives a corrupted save

modules.name: Getting Data From Elsewhere
modules.objective: Fetch data from an API and display it, including when it fails.
lessons: What an API is, without the jargon
Making a request and reading the response
When the request fails, and what the user sees
Keys, secrets and what never goes in a web page
practice: Handle seven API responses including failures
lab: Build a page powered by a public API
A working page with loading, empty and error states all handled

phases.name: Writing Code That Lasts
phases.outcome: Use version control, tests, and structure so your project survives contact with next month.

modules.name: Version Control
modules.objective: Track changes, undo mistakes, and never lose work again.
lessons: Commits: snapshots with a message that explains why
Undoing: the three things you'll actually need
Branches, and working on something without breaking what works
Putting it somewhere that isn't your laptop
practice: Recover from eight version-control situations
lab: Put your project under version control properly
A repository with meaningful commit history and a working remote

modules.name: Checking Your Own Work
modules.objective: Write tests that tell you when you break something.
lessons: Testing by hand, and why it stops scaling
Testing the edges rather than the middle
A test that would fail if the code were wrong
Running tests without thinking about it
practice: Write tests for eight functions
lab: Add a test suite to your project
A suite where every test has been shown to fail against a broken version

modules.name: Organising a Project
modules.objective: Structure a project so you can find things and change one part safely.
lessons: When one file stops being enough
Splitting code into modules with a reason
Naming files and folders for the person who arrives later
Configuration and the values that change per environment
A README that lets someone else run it
practice: Restructure seven messy projects
lab: Restructure your project and write its README
A restructured project a stranger could clone and run from the README alone

modules.name: Reading Other People's Code
modules.objective: Understand code you didn't write well enough to change it.
lessons: Where to start in an unfamiliar project
Following one thing through the code
Knowing when you don't understand it yet
practice: Answer eight questions about an unfamiliar codebase
lab: Make one change to a project you didn't write
A working change plus a written account of how you found where to make it

modules.name: Debugging Properly
modules.objective: Find the cause of a bug by narrowing it down, not by guessing.
lessons: Reproduce it reliably before you fix anything
Narrowing down: halving the search space
Printing values versus using a debugger
The bug that's in your assumption, not your code
Writing a test that captures the bug
practice: Diagnose eight bugs by narrowing
lab: Find and fix three seeded bugs in a real project
Three fixes, each with a regression test and a written diagnosis

phases.name: Getting It Onto the Internet
phases.outcome: Deploy a real project, keep it running, and handle the things that break after launch.

modules.name: Deploying
modules.objective: Put a project on the internet at a real address.
lessons: Deploying a static site, start to finish
Build steps and what happens to your code on the way
Environment variables and secrets in production
A custom domain, and what it costs
practice: Diagnose seven failed deployments
lab: Deploy your project to a real URL
A live URL anyone can visit, with the build reproducible from a fresh clone

modules.name: When You Need a Backend
modules.objective: Know what has to happen on a server and what doesn't.
lessons: Client and server: who does what
Things that cannot happen in the browser
practice: Decide client or server for eight features
lab: Add a small backend to your project
A working endpoint your front end calls, with its secret kept server-side

modules.name: Users and Accounts
modules.objective: Understand what letting people log in actually commits you to.
lessons: What an account really requires of you
Passwords: never storing what you don't have to
Using an existing auth service instead of building one
The data you are now responsible for
practice: Judge seven account-handling decisions
lab: Add authentication using an existing service
Working sign-in with a written note on what data you now hold and why

modules.name: After Launch
modules.objective: Keep a live project working, including when you haven't looked at it for a month.
lessons: Knowing it broke before a user tells you
Logs, and what to put in them
Dependency updates and the ones that matter
Coming back to your own project after eight weeks
practice: Triage seven production incidents
lab: Set up monitoring and a maintenance routine
Monitoring that would notify you, plus a written monthly maintenance routine

modules.name: Capstone — Build and Ship Something Real
modules.objective: Take an idea of your own from nothing to a deployed, tested, documented project.
lessons: Choosing a project you can actually finish
Cutting scope until it fits your real capacity
Building in stages that each work
Finishing: the last 10% nobody warns you about
practice: Cut seven over-scoped project ideas down to shippable
lab: Ship your capstone project
A deployed project with tests, a README, version history and a written build account

phases.name: Where This Goes Next
phases.outcome: Turn a working skill into a direction — freelance, employed, or building your own things.

modules.name: Showing What You Can Do
modules.objective: Present your work so someone can tell in two minutes that you can build things.
lessons: A project page that explains the decisions
Writing about a project without underselling it
practice: Rewrite seven weak project descriptions
lab: Build your portfolio page
A live portfolio with three projects, each explained in terms of decisions made

modules.name: Learning the Next Thing
modules.objective: Learn a new tool or framework on your own, without a course.
lessons: Learning by building the smallest real thing
Choosing what to learn and what to ignore
Frameworks: what they buy and what they cost
Knowing when you know enough to start
practice: Plan the learning path for seven goals
lab: Learn one new tool by building with it
A small working project in a tool you didn't know a week ago, plus your learning notes

modules.name: Working With Other People
modules.objective: Collaborate on code without meetings, and take feedback on your work.
lessons: Pull requests and asking for review
Receiving a critical review without flinching
Reviewing someone else's code kindly and usefully
Contributing to an open source project
Async collaboration on your own hours
practice: Write review comments on seven changes
lab: Make one contribution to a real project
A submitted pull request to a project you don't own, with the review addressed

modules.name: Getting Paid for This
modules.objective: Understand the realistic routes from this skill to money, and their trade-offs.
lessons: The routes: employed, freelance, product, and the honest odds
What a junior role actually asks for
First paid work: small, scoped and real
Working at variable capacity and saying so
practice: Assess seven opportunities for fit and risk
lab: Write your own next-six-months plan
A plan with a chosen route, three concrete steps and what would change your mind

modules.name: Keeping Going
modules.objective: Build a practice that survives bad weeks, long gaps and losing momentum.
lessons: Coming back after a month away
Projects designed to be picked up cold
The comparison problem, and what to do about it
What you'd tell yourself at lesson one
practice: Design a return-from-gap routine for seven situations
lab: Write your own restart protocol
A written protocol for restarting after a gap, tested by actually taking a break and using it
